subtopic: AMENDMENT AND CONSOLIDATION

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, March 16, consideration of the motion of Mr. Harris (Grey-Bruce) for the second reading of Bill No. 79, respecting Indians.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AND CONSOLIDATION
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?

subtopic: AMENDMENT AND CONSOLIDATION
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
Before the motion carries there are several matters I probably ought to mention as the bill progresses.
As I think everyone in the house realizes, Canada's 136,000 Indians, scattered from ocean to ocean, constitute to us in this parliament an urgent and inescapable challenge. Our Indians are potentially either a magnificent asset or a menacing liability. By what means, and with the greatest likelihood of ultimate success, can we aid our Indians to make themselves the priceless partners both Indians and non-Indians fervently desire to see them become? I feel that the Indian Act as it is now before the house is a great improvement over what we had a year ago. I have a letter from one of the prominent Indian leaders in Canada in which he says that Bill No. 79 has removed at least seventy-five per cent of the objections the Indians had to Bill No. 267 hardly a year ago.
I want to congratulate the minister on this achievement. The letter to which I refer

comments upon the increasing sympathy and understanding displayed by the minister towards the Indians during the months he was meeting and discussing this matter with them. As I expected, the minister has great potentialities as a statesman. His youth and inexperience in the department might have plunged him into many difficulties which a year of careful study of the problem would have helped him to avoid, and have helped him to avoid. I believe it is a source of satisfaction to the minister himself that Bill No. 267 did not go through. I am sure that the Indians throughout Canada are far more likely now to have that magnificent future to which I referred than they would have been had the bill gone through less than a year ago.
There are still several matters which should be given careful thought as we progress in the study of the Indian problem. Some of them cannot be suitably dealt with in any Indian act, but must be considered by the department more or less apart from the Indian Act.
Among the many problems which confront us in respect of the Indians, there are four which stand out particularly, and to these I should like to refer specifically.
The first problem has to do with what we might call the psychological attitude of the Indians throughout Canada. There remains in most Indians a lack of confidence. The minister has dispelled much of that, but there are still the results of years and years of what we must call mismanagement of Indian affairs in Canada. This lack of confidence must be removed. I am sure that the minister recognizes that as readily as any other man in the house, perhaps more readily.
The second problem is one of education. I am sure that no Indian act can deal suitably with the problem of Indian education. It is an exceedingly difficult problem with which to cope, for many reasons. It is, though, a problem which must be grappled with and mastered. I see no reason why the education of the children of 136,000 Indian people in Canada cannot be taken care of as efficiently and satisfactorily as we are now taking care of the education of non-Indian boys and girls in Canada. Until this educational problem has been properly met, I fear we are not likely to lay the foundation of that stable superstructure which we hope to build.
The third problem is that of rehabilitation. One of the greatest dreads that the Indians have arises from the fact that if by any chance they should be excluded from the protection of the reservations and the treaties they would not be equipped to compete with the white man on anything like equal terms. Obviously in order to build up the
Indian Act
Indian population as partners in the great Canada to be, we simply must make adequate provisions for the rehabilitation of the Indians. By that I mean that we must enable the Indian to learn how to make his living, much as the Caughnawaga Indians have done. Many of these are able to compete in the structural steel industry with any white man on the American continent. I can see no reason why we cannot so train our Indians; the problem must be grappled with and solved.
The fourth problem is that of teaching the Indians to govern themselves, or of guiding, protecting and advising them while they learn to do so. It is something which we desire they shall learn to do.
I believe these four problems are not even successfully approached in the present Indian Act. As I have indicated, I doubt that they could be. However, while we are at this business of providing something like a satisfactory arrangement for our Indians, we must not forget these four problems.
May I just mention one or two considerations in relation to the matter of increasing Indian confidence. In times past I have suggested that we should have an Indian claims commission to go into all the various problems which the Indians have in their hearts. Here is an example of the kind of thing which must be met and dealt with. I am not sure that I should give the name of the reservation involved; I have thought about it for some little time, and I am inclined to believe I should omit naming the reservation on the floor of the house, but I will give it to the minister personally. Unless the members desire particularly that the name of the reservation be given, I shall not give it. Some of the things that are said in this communication to me cast a great deal of reflection upon a great many men who are not in a position to defend themselves, and it may thereby cause some injustice; but this is what is said concerning this particular reservation:
In the first place, this reserve covered a very large territory which comprised a great amount of spruce and fir lumber, also hardwood; but the reserve was allowed to be sold off by degrees-not only sold off, but different political parties were allowed to go in and take lumber at different stump-age rates. The reserve has now lost seven-eighths of territory of what it was when the reserve was set up, and the Indian population of the reserve has doubled, with hardly sufficient timber left to furnish firewood for the Indians now on the reserve. The lumber has been completely taken from the reserve.
On investigating I discovered that the relief given the Indians was not in any way adequate to their needs. The Indians of eastern Canada have no treaty fund on which to draw. They depend on the vote of relief from parliament from year to year. There was a small hospital on the reserve, but there

Indian Act
were only one or two rooms available for patients outside of the staff and the teachers in the schools on the reserve.
I am just quoting excerpts from the statement. It continues:
So far as I can learn, this reserve has been used as a political football, and everything is operated on a patronage basis. The clothing, food and everything is to be supplied by someone who has the patronage for this part of the constituency.
Whether or not the details concerning this reservation will justify the statements which my communicant makes, certainly when a responsible man makes such statements as these, they should be examined with the minutest care.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AND CONSOLIDATION
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
Where is this
reserve?

subtopic: AMENDMENT AND CONSOLIDATION
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
I could easily give the name, but I gave reasons why I thought it would be better not to state it. There will be men involved, probably men right in this house, who will perhaps not be able to satisfactorily answer the allegations. If it is desired I can give the name in the committee, but after what I have already said I think that I should not give the name of the reserve to the house and to the country. I shall give it to the minister.
I imagine that if we were to go from ocean to ocean in Canada we would find dozens of cases at least as bad as the one I have cited. Will someone tell me how in the world the minister, with his overworked department,-and no matter how large his department is, it will be overworked-can possibly do justice to these many cases which have grown up through scores of years, unless a claims commission is set up?
If an Indian claims commission were appointed with authority to proceed with an absolutely free hand, the only demand upon them being to ascertain what was just, and to suggest how the injustice which the Indians have suffered could be removed, that would be the kind of thing I have in mind.
There are a great many other things. I will just mention one more. I do not believe it would be well at the present time for me to go into details; all that I need to do for the members of the house is to hold up this file of documents which I have on my desk, all bearing on the matter I am going to talk about, and I think they will all see that there is a great deal that can be said. I would rather have time to go into it with care before I do anything more than make a few remarks in a general way.
I refer now to the situation which confronts us with respect to the Six Nations Indians. The Six Nations Indians appear to believe,

as a matter of religion and of history, that their organization was founded by the Great White God to whom I referred in one of my previous speeches. Because of that they believe that their hereditary chiefs are men Clothed with hereditary authority of the highest possible kind. They maintain that in 1924-and they submit documentary evidence to prove what they maintain-men representing the department of Indian affairs in Ottawa violated their privileges by entering their-what word shall I use? I was going to say "sacred" but that is hardly the right word-their buildings where they kept their records, seizing those records and subjecting certain of their respectable leaders to indignities which in the minds of these people amount to an outrage.
How can the minister possibly arrive at the facts concerning this matter? When we remember that the Six Nations Indians constitute by far the most influential, well-organized and, we might say, powerful group of Indians in Canada, I think we shall realize that until we can satisfy the Six Nations Indians that justice has been done them to make up for all the unfairness they have suffered, we have not really placed ourselves on a sound foundation in constructing an Indian affairs set-up which will endure. I will say no more about the necessity for an Indian claims commission, although the information I have at my disposal would occupy several speeches, each as long as Mr. Speaker could possibly allow me to make.
May I now turn for a few minutes to the matter of education? The members of the house as a whole are familiar with the problem which confronts us in relation to Indian education. I would imagine that the majority of the members of the Indian affairs committee would agree that, properly speaking, education of Indians is a matter which properly ought to come under the direction of the provinces. If the Indians are to be placed on a basis comparable with that which obtains among their non-Indian fellows, they also must come under the provinces in the matter of education.
But no province in Canada is prepared to assume responsibility for the education of the Indians without adequate monetary compensation and guarantee. This puts the department at Ottawa in a difficult position. I want the minister to realize that I recognize that fact. But that fact does not remove the insistence of the demand that there shall be adequate treatment of the Indian educational problem. If the department must hand over the throttle, so to speak, in respect of money and say to the provinces "You solve this problem of Indian education and we

will give you almost a blank cheque while you do it", it will have to do just that. Unless the dominion is ready to do that, I do not see how we are going to solve the problem of the education of the Indians. I am sure that any province in this dominion will gladly assume that responsibility and will admirably discharge it if provided with the funds with which to do the job.
We must not expect to get education for our Indian boys and girls as cheaply as we get education for our white boys and girls. We know how costly it is to educate our non-Indian boys and girls. We must expect it to be much more costly to educate adequately the Indian boys and girls, and we must be prepared to stand right up and face that fact. I know that it is rather trite to speak in the house about what I am going to mention, but when we face a $5 billion appropriation for war for three years, we should not be too mercenary when it comes to making provision for the education of the great Indian people that is to be. One hundred and thirty-six thousand Indians in seventy-five years will be a large proportion of our Canadian population-not a body of men and women who can be disregarded in any respect or skimped in their treatment.
The problem of education remains to be solved. The minister will be virtually as helpless in his attacks on this problem as previous ministers have been, no matter how earnest and eager to solve it he may be, unless we put an adequate financial guarantee behind him. He must not have to go before the cabinet and before the treasury board and, I was going to say, break his heart in a vain effort to get them to loosen up and give him the money with which to do the job. That is just stating the facts in a simple way.
We now come to the matter of rehabilitation of the Indians. As I indicated, that means teaching the Indians how to live in the environment in which they dwell. This morning, while I was meditating on this speech, I was thinking of how, when I was a small boy, the Indians would come to visit our home, as they did the homes of most non-Indian people in the neighbourhood, just out of friendliness. The Indians were fine, friendly and co-operative people, as I knew them. They were altogether different from the Indians in the United States, because they had been treated much more fairly and honourably than the Indians in the United States had been treated. Whenever an Indian came to our home, we were fairly sure he knew how to tan a hide; almost no matter how long the hide had been off the animal,
Indian Act
you could turn it over to the Indian, and he would go and tan it and make a good job of it.
I was wondering if there is any reason why the Indian could not be taught to do the necessary work in the tanning of leather and in the making of shoes. How skilful they were in making mocassins with the most meagre equipment with which to do it! I remember the works of art and efficiency which the Indians used to produce and bring to my parents to offer for sale; I refer to the mocassins beautifully trimmed with beads artistically placed on them. People whose ancestors were able to do such work over sixty years ago surely can be taught to do almost any kind of handicraft work with great skill and efficiency. Why should they not, if they were guided by vocational directors, acquire any kind of skill which they would need in order to fit into our everyday economic life? Why should Indians not be most skilful electricians, plumbers, shoemakers, garage men, mechanics generally, and so on all through the list?
There is another thing that has always been a conundrum to me. When the Indians came to our home, no matter what was wrong with us

and we had plenty wrong with us, struggling as we were under trying conditions in those old pioneer days, when we could not give much thought to having the kind of food we needed; we were lucky if we could get enough to keep body and soul together-they knew what to do. If it was in the summertime they would go out and go down to the brook, and the first thing we knew they would come back with several different kinds of herb. They would put these together and they would often cure whatever was wrong with us almost with astonishing skill. They knew the poultices and they knew the medicines generally. The Indians must have had remarkable skill in the matter of medicine. Why should we not have more Indian doctors today? We already have a number of our girls from the Indian reservations learning to be fine nurses. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I do not think the minister will find it an impossible task to rehabilitate the Indians and to teach them to be perfectly successful in competition with the white man in almost any vocation that you could name by which the white man makes his living.
All that is necessary is to have someone who understands the Indian and is sympathetic with him, who has money enough at his disposal to send the Indian boys and girls to technological schools and all that sort of thing. I do not think there will be any difficulty in rehabilitating the Indian financially. And just as soon as the Indians are sure that they can step out into the paths of

Indian Act
the white man and make their way much of the anxiety which inhibits them today, and which fills them almost with consternation, will be dispelled as a mist on a July morning. Therefore I think we can approach this problem with complete confidence if we will just go about it in the right way.
That covers education and rehabilitation. Now, the fourth problem I mentioned, and which I shall deal with only briefly, is that of teaching the Indians or helping the Indians to learn to govern themselves. I do not think there will be any difficulty in that sort of thing if we just go about it right, with the advice that we can get from men skilled in Indian affairs. But the problem has to be solved.
One group of Indians who live on a reservation not very far from where I live-not the one that is in my constituency-asked me, "By all means"-I can see them now with the greatest concern on their faces- "let us ourselves have charge of the education of our boys and girls and we will see that they will get the training they need. We want our boys and girls to be as skilful as the white men are. We know their problems. Let us have a hand in it. Put the money and the facilities at our disposal, under the direction of white men, if you wish, but let us determine how we are going to do it."
I am not saying that that group of Indians would succeed, but they certainly believe they can succeed, and where they honestly believe they can succeed I am prepared to give them a chance. They would make mistakes, but it is the God-given right of any man in government to make a mistake. Should they make mistakes and learn by those mistakes they will feel far stronger and far more satisfied.
I do not think I need to say much more about the matter of allowing the Indians to govern themselves. Remember, they did it for 2,000 years or more before the white man came. They went to war a great deal and had many troubles like a good many others, but the Six Nations Indians had pretty well cleared up the difficulties of war among themselves. As far as I can learn the Six Nations had rather an effective government which they possibly formed themselves. If we build on the basis of what they had achieved in the past, on what they think they can do now, I believe we shall have staunch and happy allies in the Indians, and real partners in the building of this commonwealth we are working for.
How shall we go about it? With the limited amount of attention that I have been able to give this matter, struggling along as all
[Mr. Blackmore.l
other hon. members are, coping with the scores of different problems, it seems to me that it would be advisable for us to have two commissions. One of these should be an Indian claims commission. Before that commission the Indian could present his case and take it to court, if need be. He would be sure that when he had a case it would be heard, and that the decision would be just.
I believe there should be a rehabilitation commission also, quite independent of the department. As nearly as I can make out the department of Indian affairs is largely an administrative department. It has been beset with all sorts of worry, and I have the greatest sympathy for the men who have struggled with the Indian problem in times past, but it is not -a department that can get out and find facts in all cases, weigh those facts satisfactorily, and draw suitable conclusions, as a royal commission would be able to do. If we had a rehabilitation commission to take charge of the education and the training of Indian boys and girls to meet the competition of the world before them, and the providing of funds for those on land to establish farms and herds and to engage in sawmilling and things of that kind by which they could make their living, I believe that commission would do a highly gratifying job for our generation and the generations yet to come.
I do not know but that it would be a good thing to let the Indian claims commission enter into the problem of teaching the Indians to govern themselves. It may probably be better to teach the Indians to govern themselves under the rehabilitation commission, but certainly I believe we shall never succeed in this country in dealing with the Indians adequately until we do have at least two commissions just as effective as our transport commission and just as efficient as our wheat board is or the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is. These two will have just as much responsibility and authority. Probably it will cost just as much money, or a good deal more, but they would do the job if-we had the right men. Probably the best thing to suggest is to have two commissions, one the Indian claims commission and the other the rehabilitation commission.
May I close, Mr. Speaker, by reading one more compliment to the minister? It is an excerpt from a news report of a meeting in Macleod, Alberta, that appears in a recent issue of the Lethbridge Herald. The minister will recognize the two chiefs who are speaking, and he will know that out there they are saying just what they feel. The excerpt reads:
Bill 79, the new federal government bill dealing with Indian affairs, meets the wishes of the Indians

by about 75 per cent, Chief James Gladstone told the gathering in speaking of his meeting in Ottawa at the end of February with other Indian delegates to confer with Citizenship Minister Walter Harris, sponsor of the legislation.
"It was the first time in the history of Canada that Indians from Halifax to Vancouver had gathered to discuss their problems with the government," Chief Gladstone stated. "I thought it was the sublimest moment of my life," he said.
He paid tribute to Mr. Harris as the first minister at the head of Indians affairs to search out the viewpoint of the Indian. The Indian has to be educated before Bill 79 can be applied in its entirety, he said.
"It may take a generation," Chief Gladstone stated. "If the vote was forced on us now the Indian would not know how to meet it. We want to be Indians, always Indians, even though we gradually take full responsibility as Canadian citizens," he declared.
"We listened to Mr. Harris and we feel that what we get will be gradual," Chief Gladstone said. "We will have to satisfy him that we can handle it first," he stated.
Chief Albert Many Fingers, Chief Gladstone's fellow' delegate, stated the Indian's first need is education and that there is a need of day schools. The two chiefs stated the government is apparently willing to improve upon the education facilities of the Indians.
I believe that that will be valuable not only to the minister but to the members of the house who address themselves to this problem, as an indication that much progress has been made. I am of the opinion that we can make just as much progress in the next year by the earnest, tactful efforts of the minister as was made during the last year. I would not be surprised to see that he may find it advisable to adopt the suggestion which I have tentatively made concerning commissions, which will find the facts, weigh them, sift them, organize them and present them to him so that he, with his fine skilful officials to assist him, can make the necessary decisions to present to parliament.
Out of all this I believe we shall be able to say honestly, and confidently that we in our generation shall have done our bit for the Indians; that we shall have done all we can to give them the square deal they deserve.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the introduction of this bill justifies the attitude taken by many of us last summer, when we expressed the view that the inadequacies in the bill then presented were such that it should be redrafted and changed, and that so far as possible the Indians should be again consulted. I agree with the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) that the minister, in calling together representatives of the Indians from one end of the country to the other, has done much to make this measure more acceptable than any proposals of the kind we have had in the past. That is to say, the Indians will feel that they themselves have had some influence in
Indian Act
formulating policies which will come into effect as a result of this measure.
No matter how good an Indian Act we may have, it seems to me the principal problem is one of administration, involving the raising of the standards of education, health and living, and the standard of citizenship-of a new type, of course-among the Indians. I hope that what the hon. member for Lethbridge said a few moments ago toward the end of his speech will be said of this generation both by the Indian people and by the people of Canada generally. But if this generation fails to the extent that previous generations of Canadians have failed in doing justice to the original inhabitants of this country, then indeed we shall not deserve much praise. On the contrary, as a generation, we shall deserve only condemnation.
I have often thought it strange that after something like one hundred and eighty years since the first reserves were established in Canada, and now after about eighty-four years since confederation, we have living among us a depressed people, a people who have the attributes to make a contribution to our country, a people capable of enjoying standards of living and education as high as those of the white population with whom they dwell.
There have been evidences that it is possible that our Indians are capable of enjoying high standards of living and of education. For years many men and women of Indian descent have occupied important positions in Canada. I am not thinking only of those who have been full-blooded descendants of the original inhabitants of our country; I am thinking as well of those who have had high percentages of Indian blood in them. I think of a chief justice in one of our western provinces. I think of people of Indian descent who have occupied positions in various churches, and who have occupied posts in the Department of National Defence. Indeed I believe one of these attained the rank of brigadier in the first world war, and today is a respected magistrate in the second largest city of Canada.
Some years ago I had the opportunity of seeing some of the Indian schools. At that time I was fairly familiar with educational standards and age groups, and I remember being struck by the fact that the intelligence of the average Indian child in primary grades measured well with the average white child in primary grades in the ordinary common schools of the country.
Then something seemed to happen. They went back-indeed, they were encouraged to go back-to their old conditions. Gradually their condition reverted, and no further

Indian Act
attempt was made to provide opportunities for them to develop the aptitudes about which the hon. member for Lethbridge spoke. That they have those aptitudes is certain.
I know the Indian Act does not deal in any respect with Eskimos. I have been told, however, on more than one occasion that when airfields were established in Eskimo regions of the far north it was discovered that the Eskimos had aptitudes that in some instances were above those of the white men who were associating with them. As engineers they learned rapidly about the mechanism of even complicated machines such as airplane engines. Intelligence tests given to Indian children in North America show that, if tests are based upon the environmental experience of those involved, those children have as high intelligence as any of the white children.
I have often compared our record in Canada with that of the white settlers in New Zealand. When I say this I am not thinking of New Zealand under a Labour government, but of New Zealand in the long years before that government took office. In the early part of the last century-yes, indeed, approaching the second half of the last century-the original inhabitants of New Zealand were cannibals. They were not cannibals in the sense in which some other tribes were, as a matter of ritual; they were cannibals because they liked human flesh. As a matter of fact some of the missionaries who went out there became food for the Maoris. I remember well that in the city in which I was educated a memorial pulpit was erected in the cathedral to the memory of a missionary who was killed by the Maoris in 1845 or 1846. We were told that he or some of his colleagues had been consumed by them.
Yet, when parliamentary institutions were established in New Zealand in 1856, followed by fifteen years of struggle with the Maoris, we find that in 1871 they were given the franchise, and that four Maoris were elected to the parliament of that country. Today the Maoris are not assimilated-and in this country no one wants to assimilate the Indian -but they are integrated into the New Zealand community. Their sons have occupied high positions in the army, the air force, the church and the state, and have served in cabinets of the Dominion of New Zealand. Yet after nearly 200 years, after eighty-four years since confederation, our Indians in the main, with the exception of the Caughnawaga reserve, the Brant reserve and one or two other places notably in British Columbia, present a picture of economic and social depression, lacking sufficient educational facilities, living under health conditions that

are a reflection on the whole of our country with tuberculosis, though the incidence has been greatly reduced lately, still taking a relatively greater toll than among the white population in the same areas.
These are indications not of the failure of the Indians but of the failure of the white settlers of Canada to do what should have been done for this intelligent, one-time physically fit and loyal aboriginal population of this country. I agree with the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) that much depends on the education of the Indian child. I do not think that our educational efforts among the Indians have been successful. I know many of the Indians regard that as one of our greatest failures. That was brought out again and again when the committee was sitting. They desire that educational opportunities for their children shall be provided in a greater, more comprehensive and more efficient manner than before, comparable in all respects to those provided for Canadian children generally.
After all, these people are capable of independence, of initiative, of making a contribution to the cultural, economic and social life of the country in which we live, and they have been denied that opportunity. To a very large extent I think that is due to the fact that our attitude has been purely paternalistic, and the Indian Act has been administered purely from the paternalistic point of view. Not enough opportunity has been given to the Indian population to guide their own destinies and to raise their standards of life and of living.
When we look at the way in which their old treaty rights have been set aside, forgotten or impinged upon, that also is a reflection on our good faith as a people in our dealings with the Indian population. Therefore, while I think that the bill is a distinct improvement over the old Indian Act, while it is an improvement over the bill that was presented to us last summer, nevertheless it is defective in that it perhaps has not sufficient vision in the realm of education and, I regret to say, in the realm of health of the Indians. I would have liked to see more direct control of health facilities among the Indians placed in the Indian department, although I am not for one moment belittling the great improvement that has been made since the present Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) took over the supervision of that department. I think there has been a very great improvement, and I want to say that; but we are concerned with the standards of living and the social rehabilitation, if you like to call it such, of the Indian people.

There are two fields that need particular attention, health and education, and to a large extent the two go together, education for health, health for education. Consequently 1 would like to see more attention to the problem of health and welfare in the bill. However, as I have already said, the bill is an improvement over the one introduced last year. I hope that in the administration of the new act every attempt will be made to raise the standards of the Indians and to use those aptitudes that they have in such large measure to enable them to enter upon vocations and ways of life that will not only help them to improve their physical and economic-conditions but also enable them to make a contribution to the cultural life of our country and which will gradually bring about the integration-not assimilation-of the Indian population into the general population of Canada.
I think the whole basis of our thought over the last number of years with respect to racial and other differences in our country has not been to try to make all Canadians of the same pattern of speech, thinking, religion or culture, but rather that each particular group in Canada, whether they be English, Scots, French, Ukrainian or whatever they may be, by preserving their cultural heritage, may contribute together to the making of a Canadian culture which will be not of one sort, kind or pattern but rather like a mosaic, a picture composed of many different types of stone or, in the words I have just used, of many cultures. Therefore I welcome the bill as an improvement. But no bill, no matter how good, will succeed unless we have a minister, and a department manned by officials, who have a high ideal and who are determined not to keep on treating the Indians as children but as human beings who have capabilities which, if given scope, will enable them to make a contribution not only to their own welfare but to the welfare of the country in which they and we hope to live together in unity for generations to come.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to take only three or four minutes in discussing the bill at the present time inasmuch as I have spoken in the house many times in the past about Indian affairs, and I do not wish to repeat what I said on those occasions. Second, a good deal of what I might otherwise have said has already been said by speakers who have preceded me. Needless to say, I welcome the introduction of the bill at a fairly early stage in the session when we will have time to consider it without being pressed to get it through so
Indian Act
that the session may end. That is one great advantage, so far as the timing of the introduction of the bill is concerned, over the one which was introduced last year.
I am sorry that I was not able to be here when the minister made his speech introducing the bill. However, I have read it carefully and by and large I agree with the general tenor and spirit of the speech he made on March 16 last. The steps he mentioned in that speech as having being taken to obtain the opinion of the Indians and others across Canada interested in the welfare of the Indians I think were exceptionally good and have had fruitful results, as indicated by the changes that have been made in this act. That is also indicated, if I may say so, by the different attitude being displayed by the minister this year as compared with last year, for which I commend him. I believe the steps taken to obtain the views of the Indians were extremely important as far as the psychological effect upon the Indians themselves was concerned. They feel they are in on the thing now, that they have been consulted, and that some weight has been given their opinions. If any Indian act is to work I think one of the essentials is that the Indians themselves have some confidence in it, and are able to feel that they had a hand in framing it.
In the same way I think it was an excellent move to bring Indian representatives from across Canada to Ottawa for a conference, as was done at the end of February and the beginning of March of this year. I was glad to learn from the minister's speech that such a large degree of unanimity existed among those representatives. The situation as far as Indians are concerned differs greatly as between the various parts of the country, so it is almost impossible to bring in any act that will please everybody. Of course I do not suppose any act of any kind ever pleases everyone; but because of the great difference between living conditions among Indians in the maritimes and those on the prairies, for instance, what may suit one group will not suit another. So I hope this will be taken into consideration and there will be some flexibility in the application of this act.
In my opinion a number of clauses in the present bill could still be improved. Some of them I would say will prove unacceptable to the majority of the Indians when they see them in operation, even though a majority of their representatives did not oppose them at the conference. I should hope that when this bill is considered in committee the minister and his officials will not take an inflexible attitude toward amendments to various clauses. I believe the bill can be

Indian Act
further improved, and I sincerely trust that in the committee every effort will be made to bring about those improvements. I see the minister nodding his head, which is a good sign.
I do not want to go into the various clauses at this time. Particularly do I not want to draw down upon my head your ire, Mr. Speaker, for transgressing the rules. However, I should like to make reference to one or two of the provisions which I think are not acceptable and in which I hope some changes may be made. The first is section 4 (2) in connection with the power of the governor in council to abolish Indian reserves, or to abolish the Indian status as far as an individual is concerned. That has been referred to already, so I need say no more about it. One thing which needs revision, which is still unsatisfactory, is the definition of an Indian, which takes up several clauses of the bill. I would agree with the statement by the minister, I think it was last year, that the business of defining an Indian is extremely difficult. It is very hard to draw up a definition that is simple and at the same time more or less all-inclusive. The definition in the old act was comparatively simple. The definition in this bill, as I say, is far from simple, running through a considerable number of clauses; and I think it is quite bad in some respects. Then the matter of the disposal of children is something else in which I believe there could be a change for the better, and I trust something will be done in that regard.
One paragraph in the minister's speech disturbed me to some extent. At page 1352 he said:
I received many letters from people saying: There is nothing whatever in the bill about old age pensions for Indians. Similarly there were many letters saying: You have not provided in the bill that, wherever possible, an Indian child should obtain the same standard of education that a non-Indian receives. The house will readily understand why those matters are not contained in the bill. Those are matters which are provided for in this house by votes in the estimates and not by legislation.
The reason that disturbed me is that in 1945, when I first came into the house, I moved a resolution asking that the government take into consideration the payment of the old -age pension to Indians. That resolution was debated for at least a day, and at the end of the day the then Minister of Mines and Resources stated that it should be allowed to stand because they proposed, and he promised, that a committee would be set up to consider Indian affairs and that as a result amendments would be made to the act. So he did not think anything could be done about paying old age pensions until the committee had met and the act had been

amended. That has been more or less the answer ever since, except that last year a payment was introduced which was supposed to be in lieu of old age pensions. Ever since 1945 the story given us has been that old age pensions could not be paid to Indians until this act was amended; but now the act has been amended this statement would seem to indicate that old age pensions are still not to be paid.
I do not think it is much use for the minister to say that this matter should be dealt with in the estimates unless he is prepared to deal with it in that way. We on this side of the house certainly cannot put anything in the estimates for the payment of old age pensions; and if they are not provided under the Indian Act by statutory authority, it means that they can only be paid- if the minister or the government decides to put an item in the estimates. Personally I would much rather see this thing settled by a provision in the act that the Indians shall be treated, in the matter of old age pensions, just as other citizens of Canada are treated. That is all that would be required, one short clause added to the act. Then we would have the statutory authority for equality of treatment for the Indians in that regard.
The situation is the same as far as education is concerned. I know that is not something which can be written into the act, however; and I must say that during the last four years in particular there has been a very considerable improvement in education as far as the Indians are concerned. However, I would like to have more definite assurance in regard to what we might call a policy of educational opportunities equal to those afforded white children, as far as that may be possible. The only reason I say that is that some of the Indians in the more remote areas of this country will not, for some considerable length of time, be able to have equal educational opportunities with the white children in the more populous areas. As has been indicated by other speakers, this matter of the education of Indians is perhaps the most important question in so far as the handling of our Indian problem is concerned. As was stated by the member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) a short time ago, only by providing improved educational facilities can the Indians possibly be integrated with the rest of our population.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are one or two general remarks on this subject which I should like to take the opportunity of emphasizing at this time. Practically no statement which can be made, in this house or elsewhere, about Indians could be correctly applied to

all the Indians in Canada. There is an almost unbelievable difference between the state of their educational and financial advancement in the various parts of the country, so that it is impossible to say that the Indian is this or the Indian wants that. Such statements are likely to cause a great deal of misunderstanding. Not only is that true as between one part of the country and another, but in my own district, which happens to be one which represents both coastal and interior areas, the difference is almost beyond belief.
We have Indian settlements on the coast where the majority of the people living in those villages are paying income taxes on larger amounts than I ever hope to pay income tax upon, and whose homes are of a better quality than any it has yet been my privilege to have. Two hundred miles or less from those areas we have villages in which the conditions are nothing less than deplorable, and those conditions apply both to the physical circumstances under which the Indian lives and to the mental and physical condition of those Indians themselves. In trying to meet this Indian question, therefore, we must realize that we cannot adopt any hard and fast rule that applies to the Indians as a whole. No section which can be written into an act of this sort, or very few of them, can be said to apply in detail to the Indians of Canada. If such a section contains maximum or minimum provisions which apply directly to certain Indian groups, then it is certainly going to be out of place in its application to other groups.
It is as a result of that that many of the sections of this act appear to me to be safeguarded. It is because of the difference between the various Indians, as mentioned by the member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness), that these sections which are causing the greatest amount of opposition throughout the country have to be retained in the act. I believe that all legislators, and certainly all legislators who have had occasion to practise law, will realize that in many sections of acts such as the Criminal Code there are maximum penalties which are out of all proportion to the seriousness of some of the offences committed under those sections. Those maximum penalties are not there to be applied in every case. They are to be applied in the extreme cases where the person who is administering that act believes they are applicable. I submit the same rule applies to those sections which have to be retained here, where in certain cases the minister, who I presume will be acting upon the advice of his departmental officials, has certain overriding authority. It does not follow that he is going to use that authority, even if he considers it might be advisable to do so. But I
Indian Act
hope that it follows he is going to use that authority when he considers it is necessary in the interests of the Indians concerned that some act should be overridden by the power which has been retained in certain sections of this bill.
I am going to say something which could easily be misinterpreted, Mr. Speaker. It is because I submit that safeguard must be in the act to apply to the more backward and more helpless Indians, I think there is a duty on those of us who are in this house, and on the citizens of Canada who are not in this house, to discuss this matter and deal with this subject in such a way that the faith of the Indian in the government of Canada will be retained. In order to make it clear to my friends opposite, I am not referring at the moment to this government but to the government of Canada as an institution. The government of Canada as an institution is primarily responsible for protecting, as well as for advancing, the Indians of Canada. So long as they must look to that government for that protection, and for that advancement, it is certainly up to those of us who claim to have the interests of the Indian at heart to see that he looks to that overriding authority with a certain amount of faith and trust.
I assume we are all discussing this act and its administration with a view to the improvement of conditions for Indians, and not with a view to arousing agitation or opposition to the bill either amongst the Indians or the whites. I do not suppose I am the only member who has found in his district a certain inclination among some Indians and some whites to use the fact that this bill is up for discussion as an excuse to arouse a certain amount of agitation and opposition, not necessarily on party political lines at all but in order that there might be unrest in the district. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that most members in whose ridings there reside a large number of Indians, and who state that does not exist in their district, are either not very familiar with what is going on in their district or are extremely fortunate. I say with regret that in my district there are those who have not the interests of either the Indian or the Dominion of Canada at heart who are making use of this bill as an opportunity to belittle and hurt the body politic of Canada.
I should like to mention one other point in connection with the act. We must remember that administration and legislation are not the same thing. I tried to point that out at the commencement of these few remarks in my reference to the minimum and maximum. Those who are charged with the administration of the act will be the people

Indian Act
who will decide whether the maximum, the minimum or something halfway between is to be applied, and whether a permissive section must be called into account. When we look at these permissive or restrictive sections, I would urge that we remember that, while in perhaps seven-tenths of the country there may be no need for this if in one-tenth of the country there are Indians whose circumstances may make that section advisable, then the section should be allowed to remain. 'Our duty then will be to watch the administration of the act.
In my own district there are amongst the Indians two major fears. There is the fear of the Indian who has reached a considerable stage of advancement that he is going to be held down and not allowed to advance any further. There is the fear of the Indian who has reached a very low stage of advancement that he is going to have advancement forced upon him, that he is going to be gradually edged out of the comfortable situation in which he finds himself-and I use -that word "comfortable" not in its literal sense- whereby he has practically no responsibilities of his own-. He has his reserve; he has his little grants; he has a government to fall back on and he does not want advancement, and in some cases he is not being encouraged to want it.
There you have two diametrically opposed situations; and it is going to be up to the administrators of the act to raise those in the lower categories so that while we have a restrictive act to protect them we shall not deter those who are more advanced from going ahead. In other words, we must not hold back those who are well ahead until those who are far behind have caught up.
Before I sit down I believe it is my duty as spokesman for the Indians in the riding of Skeena, or at least for that large part of them who are taking an interest in these matters, to express our sincere thanks to the present Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) generally for the patience, genuine good will and sincerity which he is bringing to the whole question of the Indian Act, and specifically for calling the conference which he called from February 28 to March 3 and discussing not just Indian problems but Indian legislation with the Indians themselves.
I want to mention one other thing, Mr. Speaker, and then I am finished. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) referred in passing to a situation which did exist, and I believe still does, in New Zealand. By his reference I do not know whether he meant to imply that we should give that matter serious consideration here; I hope not. The

matter of parliamentary representation for the Indians comes under the Dominion Elections Act and not under the Indian Act. So far as the natives of New Zealand were given the vote, they were given the right to elect four, I think it is, members at large to sit in the house of parliament representing them. That idea appealed to me some time ago and I discussed it with many of our more enlightened Indians who are still on reserves in British Columbia. They told me that is the last thing they would like to see introduced in Canada. By so doing we would by statute perpetuate a differentiation in citizenship, something which is the last thing the progressive Indian wants to see.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take part briefly in the discussion relating to the amendments to the Indian Act. This is one of the problems to which there does not seem to be any definite solution. As one other hon. member has said, regardless of what you do, there will be certain ones who will not be satisfied. The suggestions I make this afternoon are not made in a critical way at all. I put them forward as suggestions in the hope that possibly through the act or the regulations under the act there will be improvement in the relations between ourselves and the Indians, and a betterment of conditions among the various tribes and bands in the country.
I think the minister was well advised when he laid over the amendment of the act until this session of the house. All parties were given an opportunity to look into it still further and those who are interested in Indian affairs were given the opportunity to have representations made to the minister.
I happen to live near a reservation and I know a considerable number of the Indians. Last week a delegation came over to see me. They said that, as far as the Indian Act was concerned, it was applying democracy in a left-handed manner. By that they meant, "we have this forced on us." That is democracy such as the totalitarian states have. I think the minister should keep that consideration in mind in the working out of the regulations under the act.
Another interesting thing that came to my attention was the fact that in 1885 the Indians were given the franchise or the vote. That is the first time. All Indians east of the province of Manitoba were given the franchise. If you look back into history you will find that was in the days of Sir John A. Macdonald. If you go into the matter still further, you will find: that in 1898 they were denied the right to vote and that situation has continued until this day except in certain cases where Indians have been in the armed

forces. In 1898 you will recall that Sir Wilfrid Laurier was in power. Those Indians who were talking to me have not forgotten that.

The minister waves his hand, but those Indians have not forgotten that. I looked the matter up in the guide and find that such is the case. In two wars they were expected to fight for the country and they did so creditably. But after they return they find that, as far as their band is concerned, they are just back where they were. That remark does not apply of course to pensions and other benefits under the veterans charter but it does apply to their status in the community. I am told that in the United States all Indians are privileged to vote in a general election.
Years ago there were disputes as to the rights of Indians freely to cross the border between the United States and Canada. I believe this was dealt with in what is referred to as the Jay treaty. But finally after many years the Indians have again been given the right to cross and recross the border freely. But some peculiar things have happened. One of them is that the Indians in my area will go across to Detroit in Michigan and secure employment; they will purchase a car which will have a Michigan licence on it. When they enter Canada, if they are not going to stay for more than a day or two, that is all right. But if they are going to stay for any length of time, they are given a permit card and they go to the reservation and are not allowed to use their car for business or pleasure while they are there. When an American tourist comes to this country, driving a United States car with a United States licence on it, he can go anywhere he likes. We welcome him for the United States dollars he brings to this country. But the Indian is not given that right.

The individual Indian has no one to whom he can go to get that corrected. He is the victim of circumstances, and therefore he feels a bit of resentment toward the department. Education along the proper lines is probably the greatest solution and the most desirable thing to have so far as the Indians are concerned.
May I point out the attitude taken and the conclusions that are arrived at by some people? The government is administering the affairs of the Indians. The delegation that came to see me wanted to know about the C.C.F. I said to them: They believe that the

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a good deal of light has been thrown upon the position of the Indians this afternoon, particularly by the hon. member who said that you could not make a rule to apply to Indians in one part of the country and expect it to apply to individual Indians in another part of the country. Up in the northern part of the Dominion of Canada there are Indians who today are living in a very primitive state, who are not settled down. They travel about the country. Their employment is seasonal. They fish during one season and hunt and trap during another season. Certain of those tribes are continuously on the move; therefore it would be very difficult to establish day schools, for instance, in that part of the country and expect the children to go to school as the white children do in Ontario or elsewhere with their school bags under their arms and then come home in the evening to mother to have their suppers, and so forth. You cannot make such rules in that part of the country.
And yet, in south Cariboo on the Fraser river you will find Indians well settled, tilling farms and conducting business in a very proper manner. You will find that these people have good incomes and good homes. I know of one group who grew tomatoes last season near Lillooet and received $400 per acre net profit on the production of that particular crop. I know of one settlement down on Seton lake in the south Cariboo country where the Indians have electric lights in their homes, and many of them have modern homes and live on standards quite equal to that of the whites.
How then can you make a rule that will apply to all of these people? There are some
3,000	of them in the riding which I represent. In the southern part, as I have said, many of them are prosperous. They do cattle ranching and conduct saw mills. They have co-operative activities in agriculture; they have co-operative stores; and it all comes about largely through the good management that this government has shown in that regard.
Day schools have been established. In my own lifetime I have seen these people emerge and progress and come up to a very good standard of citizenship in that part of our Cariboo country.
We hear a good deal of weeping about the sad plight of our Indians. Great sympathy is shown here and there. I often think they are crocodile tears, because the Indian does

not require so much of our commiseration, so much of our sympathy. Somebody referred to Sir John A. Macdonald, who was the prime minister of Canada, seeking an amendment to the Indian Act. At that time, in 1878, he proposed that the Indian be given the vote. Well, fortunately there were Liberals in the house at that time. One prominent Liberal rose and said:	"Mr. Speaker, if you give
them the vote they will just quit the scalping party and come over to the polling booth." At that time the Indians in the western part of the country particularly were living under very primitive conditions. They were savages in the truest sense. They engaged in tribal wars. They still held "scalping parties." In the annals of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police of the last few years there are reports of cannibalism up in the north, where people were reduced to poverty through bad weather and so forth. I was speaking to a man who was very well informed on this subject and he said that in the Fraser valley not very many years ago tribal wars were still going on; although the white man was there with his police and so forth, rival tribes fell upon each other and inflicted casualties whenever the opportunity arose.
As I say, they are emerging and have emerged in one or two generations from a condition of primitive people. To whom should the credit be given for lifting them up? I am speaking of my own part of the country. The credit must very largely be given to ministers of religion who worked so diligently with these people on the Mackenzie river, on the Peace river and on the Fraser river, to open up hospitals, schools and missions and to guide and help those people to the position in which they are today. As I have said, they are emerging very rapidly to a place of equality with the rest of the Canadian people. I regret I have heard in the house disparaging remarks regarding the part religion has played in the affairs of the Indians. I say the Christian missionaries who wept into that country rendered a great service to Canada and the world.
When I make that statement I am not limiting it to any one denomination. I think of the work of the Anglican church on the south Fraser river. I think of their opening schools such as the one at Lytton where several hundred Indians are in residence. I think of men like the late Rev. Archdeacon E. W. W. Pugh who came from Cambridge as a medical missionary, and who practically gave his life for the service of those people.
That was in the lower part of the Cariboo. Then, in the north the work was taken over by the Oblate missionaries. The history of the service given by the Oblate Fathers to the

Indian tribes is one of the most inspiring in the history of our country. It is going on today, and it has been going on for more than eighty years. Those missionaries are giving their lives in the conducting of schools and hospitals, and in the giving of other services to Indians. All this is being done without hope of reward, save the possibility of a crown of glory in the life hereafter.
Right up on the Cariboo highway at Fort Nelson only two winters ago Rev. Father Levesque, an Oblate missionary, went into the wilds to rescue an Indian family. He drove his dog team about eighty miles to bring service and help to those people. He froze his feet rendering that service and, as a result of it, is maimed for life. Such unselfish service is going on continuously in the part of the country I represent. I might state that Father Levesque is now in the Royal Canadian Air Force and, fortunately, is able to act as padre.
My mind turns to the Sisters of Religion at Williams Lake in the Cariboo, who conduct a hospital up there. These are Indian women of culture and education, and they take their places along with those doing similar work of any denomination or any racial group.
I think of Father A. G. Morice, who was up in Fraser Lake, at Stuart lake and at Fort St. James; of Father Lacombe, Father Seguin, and others like Father Mulvihill who is a missionary at Lejac today. I think of Rev. Father Patterson, O.M.I. of Lillooet, a native son of Perth county, Ontario, who is today assisting in organizing the co-operatives I mentioned, and in setting up credit unions and assisting Indians in co-operative saw mill and stores enterprises. In other words, he is assisting them in a material way as well as spiritually to attain their proper place in the life of the country.
I say that in bringing in this bill the minister is rendering a great service to Canada. Sir John A. Macdonald was not of the party to which I belong, but in his day he rendered heroic service. I see today a promising future for the minister who follows in the steps of great Canadian statesmen and now brings forward such progressive legislation for the benefit of the Indians and all the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, I shall take only a few moments before the bill goes to committee. I was pleased with the remarks of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) when he referred to the number of Indian people who have made a real contribution to Canadian life.
Indian Act
I see the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham) in his seat. I have no doubt the minister will be well aware of one of them as an official high up in his department who has rendered a real service and is a credit to the civil service of Canada. That man, who is serving in the minister's department, is Mr. Gilbert Monture who, I know, is recognized as an authority on minerals in the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys.
I am happy that the minister has given an extension of time for the discussion of the bill because, in looking over it, there are one or two points I find I should like to bring to his attention. Perhaps it might be done more effectively at this time than when the bill goes before the committee.
The minister has said that the Indians will be given control of their affairs when they demonstrate their ability to do so. To my mind this is an excellent approach to the problem. In the matter of the location of roads, the administration of estates of deceased persons, the handling of wills and matters of that kind the Indians can give valuable advice to the minister because they are familiar with local conditions.
It is true that many sections of the bill provide that, at the discretion of the minister, band councils are to be consulted. However, there are still several sections in which that provision does not appear, and where I think it should be included. Those sections lack the statutory authority which means so much to the Indian people. They know that if it is included in the act and brought into effect they will be recognized and be given the proper consideration.
At this point I should like to voice my objection to section 4(2)(a) and 4(2)(b). I believe that, upon reflection, the minister will agree that it does violate the principles of good citizenship, and that it is contrary to constitutional law.
All hon. members are familiar with the many sacrifices made by the Indians in the two great wars. I know that from the Six Nations Indians, located close to my home, there were five hundred who enlisted for active service. The records of those men compare favourably with those of others who took part in the war effort. I say the minister would be making a real contribution to the Indian people if he were to make provision whereby Indians could have a voice in the government of our country, without at the same time losing their identity and rights as Indians. We as Canadians are always deeply concerned about any infringement upon our rights and freedoms. I do feel that in all these

Indian Act
matters set out in the bill we must make sure that the Indians are given proper consideration in the affairs on which the government of our country legislates.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased that a measure is being offered to improve the conditions of Indians on reserves. I support the request of the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) that a commission or a committee be set up to investigate Indian reserves throughout Canada. In my view the committee headed by the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Brown) did good work in travelling throughout eastern Canada.
There are two Indian reservations in my constituency. Let me put on record the fact that the Indians of eastern Canada depend for relief upon a vote by this parliament. They have no treaty money, as do the Indians in western Canada. The Indians in the west are preferred, just as are the white people. They are a preferred class-as was clearly indicated when, before Easter, approval was given to the $65 million bonus to western farmers.
I should like to place on record the scale of the monthly ration for Indians on relief. Each adult Indian can receive flour to the value of $1.44 a month; rolled oats, 54 cents; baking powder, 30 cents; tea, $1; sugar, 22 cents; lard, 69 cents; beans, 50 cents; rice, 40 cents; cheese, 48 cents; and meat or fish, $1. Hon. members all know what one dollar will buy by way of meat or fish in a month's time. Then he is allowed ten cents' worth of salt and ten cents' worth of matches. That is all one Indian adult is allowed for a month, and it comes to $6.77. Two adult Indians are allowed $11.11 for a month. Three adult Indians are allowed $14.30. Four adult Indians are allowed $16.76. Five adult Indians are allowed $19.09. Six adult Indians are allowed $22.54, and nine, adult Indians are allowed $34.30 per month. You will notice that in this ration there are no vegetables of any kind.

There is no butter, milk or eggs. In my constituency there are lots of potatoes that are selling cheaply. There were a great many Indians on relief in that reserve a year ago. They were out of work. Many young returned veterans could not get work. Potatoes were cheap. They could be bought for 50 cents a bag of 75 pounds. Yet the agent was not allowed to give them a potato. One adult Indian could buy 40 cents' worth of rice for a month's time, but he was not allowed to have potatoes. Children were not allowed to have milk, eggs or butter. I think

the scale of monthly rations issued in Ottawa by the superintendent of welfare and training is disgraceful. It should be revised.
The Indian chief advised me that a sick Indian on his reserve, Simon Paul, had six children and is only allowed $16 per month to feed his wife and the six small children. I consider that is a disgrace. I would ask the minister to look into the question of the ration allowed Indians in eastern Canada. The answer I was given by the superintendent of welfare and training was that the Indians were supposed to grow their own vegetables. They have land on the reserve but very few of them put in a garden. If they are on relief they are not supplied with seed to grow their own vegetables, and I think they should be. When there is a large reserve with plenty of land they should be helped. A man experienced in agriculture should be put in charge of the land and the Indians should be shown how to grow their own vegetables. They should be able to grow enough vegetables on this reserve to feed all the Indians, and vegetables are the cheapest and best food that they can use.
I would impress upon the minister that he should have the regulations changed, and that on large reserves someone should be in charge of agriculture. Someone should teach the young Indians how to put in gardens and how to grow enough vegetables for their own use. I hope the amended act will be an improvement. I still submit that there should be a committee or commission to travel throughout the country looking into these different matters on the reserves.

Mr. Speaker, since the principle of the measure before the house is what is under discussion, I think it is appropriate to say something about the principle which is really inherent in what we are now discussing. Complimentary things have been said about the approach that has been made to this subject. To the extent that we accept the continuance of the present relationship between our native Indian population and the rest of the Canadian people, the statement of the minister was a commendable expression of friendship toward the descendants of the original citizens of the area that is now Canada. He indicated a desire to meet them, to hear their point of view and to improve the law now in force.
It seems to me, however, that we should have something more in mind. In so far as one can establish a principle under discussion at the moment, that principle is that we shall continue the existing relationship of the Indian to the state. In many ways the bill represents an improvement both in the

approach to the problem of the Indian and in the administrative procedure that will be brought into effect, subject to the reservation that I think section 4 is a most improper one having regard to what can be done thereunder no matter what the minister may intend to do. Nevertheless it seems to me that there is something lacking in our approach to this subject, and that it is something not only of concern to the native Indian population but also of very great concern to every Canadian who believes in the principles of individual freedom which we are asserting so continually at this particular time.
I do not think that we have any right to be satisfied with the bill. When I say that I am not suggesting that the bill may not be a great improvement over the legislation now on the statute books. What I am suggesting is that every one of us as a Canadian should feel much less than satisfied that at this point in the history of Canada we should still be dealing with a very large number of people in this country as a people with less than the regular rights of citizenship. Surely, if we are going to join in declarations that every individual throughout the world has the right to equality the place for us to start that discussion is right here at home. If it is wise for us to urge the extension of equality to the peoples of other lands, let us in this parliament assert that principle in dealing with the descendants of the original citizens of the country that we are trying to build and advance in every way within our power.
I do not believe that we should be satisfied until we can say with conviction that every Indian child has the same chance of education and advancement as every other Canadian child. Surely no one will suggest that with the passing of the bill now before us or even with such improvements as may emerge by way of amendment, with its present form and structure, we shall have even approached a point where we can declare that we have extended to the young children of native Indian blood that measure of equality which is the hall-mark of democracy itself.
Surely what we should ask ourselves is not whether it is advancing the cause of the Indians in Canada, but whether we as Canadians are satisfied to have from 130,000 to
140,000	people continuing to live in this country with less than the basic rights of citizenship which we have joined in declaring through the United Nations to be the right of human beings everywhere. In saying this I am questioning neither the motives nor the attitude of the minister towards those people with whom this legislation will deal. The drafting of the act will depend upon how we approach this subject. From the fact that
Indian Act
this bill has been presented as a government measure and will now be referred to a committee, with whatever improvement may be made there, it is obvious that what is under contemplation is a measure that perpetuates a situation which should not be satisfactory to any Canadian today. In giving this bill second reading and referring it to a committee where further discussion may take place and improvements may be made, I do hope there will be in the minds of the members of this house the hope that before long we shall achieve that measure of advancement in regard to this matter which will bring the Indians fully within the citizenship of Canada.
There is nothing in the mind of any young Indian which prevents him from absorbing education and becoming successful in this country. We have seen evidence, which has been referred to already, of the great success of educated Indians in the ordinary professional and other activities of this country. There are many examples of great achievements in the peaceful occupations of Canada. And we should remember that during the years of war the Indians of this country did their full share in preserving that freedom which should be their heritage as well as the heritage of every Canadian. They showed themselves gallant and skilled on the field of battle. They showed themselves responsible and reliable. The Indians themselves have demonstrated that if we lay the foundation for full citizenship they will be worthy of the opportunity we give them.
Motion agreed to and bill read the second time.
