speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since 1905 the Northwest Territories have been administered by a commissioner appointed by the governor in council, acting on instructions from time to time given to him by the governor in council or the minister. The Northwest Territories Act now provides for a council of six members to aid the commissioner in the administration of the territories. All the members are appointed by the governor in council. This is the form of government that has existed since 1921.
With the increase in population and the development of the territories, it is considered that there should be some elected representa-

fives in the council. It is intended, therefore, to enlarge the council to eight members, of whom three shall be elected and five appointed. Provisions are contained in the bill to authorize the establishment of three electoral districts to be represented by three elected members. There are several other minor amendments in the bill, the most important one being the granting of authority for the appointment of sheriffs.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ELECTED REPRESENTATION IN TERRITORIAL GOVERNMENT AND APPOINTMENT OF JUDICIAL OFFICERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity of saying a few words in support of the bill which will be introduced. For administration purposes the Northwest Territories were divided into three districts, namely, Mackenzie, Keewatin and Franklin, by order in council of March 16, 1918. In accordance with the Northwest Territories Act, the Northwest Territories are governed by a commissioner, a deputy commissioner, and five councillors appointed by the governor in council and operating from Ottawa. The commissioner and council have power to make ordinances for the government of the territory under instructions from the governor in council or the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters), subject to any act of the parliament of Canada applying to the territories.
Prior to confederation the land now known as the Northwest Territories was governed by the Hudson's Bay Company, and it was transferred to Canada on July 15, 1870. Upon the creation of the province of Manitoba in 1870, a single lieutenant governor performed the offices of the crown for the province and exercised a personal rule over the Northwest Territories under the direction of the federal government. He was assisted in the administration of the territories by a council not exceeding fifteen nor less than seven persons appointed by order in council. The Northwest Territories Act of 1875 provided for the administration of the territories by a resident lieutenant governor, assisted by a council of not more than five persons appointed by the governor in council, and all other members elected according to population. There were many changes in the form and size of the Northwest Territories council or legislative assembly in the succeeding years leading up to the creation of the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta in 1905.
During the years 1876 and 1877 the seat of government was at Livingston on Swan river. The capital was then transferred to Battle-ford where it remained until 1882, when Regina became the capital and remained so until the creation of the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta in 1905. Following that,

the capital was transferred to Ottawa, Since 1905 the territories have been administered by a commissioner acting under instructions of the governor in council or the Department of Resources and Development, or its preceding departments.
The commissioner has been aided by a council which, up to 1921, did not exceed four persons, and which since 1921 has not exceeded six persons. It will be noted that the Northwest Territories has been governed since 1905 by a commissioner, who was aided by a body of appointed councillors, situated at Ottawa. The great proportion of these councillors have been civil servants. No matter how able and sincere these councillors have been, this form of government is not democratic. Can you imagine eastern Ontario being governed by an appointed body of men residing and meeting on Vancouver island?
Our people feel that, while the present administrations are good and composed of able and conscientious men, the council is not in a position to deal with many of the problems of the territories as well as a similar body of elected members resident in the territories, and that in the very near future we should have responsible government throughout in keeping with the Canadian tradition of responsible government. It is admitted that the revenue found in the Northwest Territories has not been sufficient to defray the expenses of government, and the population has not been large enough to carry the cost of governmental machinery. For many years the population consisted predominantly of nomadic Indians and Eskimos, who made their living by hunting and trapping.
Since the 1920's, and especially since the end of world war II, there has been a considerable change in the situation. Industry and mining have moved into the territories, and I venture to say that many more will be moving in within the next few years to develop the vast mineral resources which are being discovered almost every day. There are the oil fields at Norman Wells along the Mackenzie river; the rich gold mines in the Yellowknife district; the uranium mine at Eldorado on Great Bear lake; the rich lead deposits at Pine Point on the south side of Great Slave lake, which I am hoping will lead to the construction of a railway; hydro developments at Fort Smith; and the nickel find at Ferguson lake in the Keewatin district. On Great Slave lake there is one of the largest inland fisheries in the world, resulting in a population of approximately 1,500 at Hay river. All this development has meant a large increase in population in the Mackenzie district.
Northwest Territories Act
It is about time that these Canadians were granted a form of local self-government similar to that enjoyed by Canadians in other parts of our country, and I am sure, Mr. Speaker, you will agree that the present form of appointed members to the Northwest Territories council can never be as good and efficient as local self-government. For this reason, Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) on introducing this bill. It is a move in the right direction towards giving complete local self-government to these people, which is the basis of our form of democracy.
I hope it will not be long before the people of the Mackenzie district of the Northwest Territories are governed in local matters by a wholly elected council which will meet in the territory, and which will consist of people who live in the territory, make their living there, and who have the interest and future of the territory at heart. This form of local self-government has worked well in the Yukon Territory for the last fifty years and more. For the life of me, I cannot see why it will not work as well in the Mackenzie district of the Northwest Territories.

Mr. Speaker, the bill before the house is comparatively simple, but since, among other things, it provides for the extension of the life of the Export and Import Permits Act, perhaps it would be appropriate for me, and the house would wish me, to say


a few words about that act, and to give some information with respect to it and to the operations under it, as well as to deal with the provisions of the bill itself.
Hon. members will recall that export control was established under the authority of the War Measures Act in 1941, and with the ending of the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act legislation was brought forward in 1947 and the Export and Import Permits Act was passed in that year, having at that time a provision in the act itself for termination in 1948. In 1948 the bill was amended and the life of the act was extended until 1950. In 1949 the life of the act was again extended until July 31, 1951, so that the present act would expire on July 31, 1951, unless extended. During all this period a continuing effort was maintained to remove items from control as quickly as the necessity for their control disappeared. At the end of the war there were 1,100 items under export control.
By October, 1950, this number had been reduced to 82 items. Unfortunately however since that time it has been necessary again to place certain items under export control. This has been by reason of the well known developments on the international scene. It was done both for domestic supply reasons within Canada and also for the reason that it was desirable to prevent this country's serving as a back door for exports from the United States. As hon. members know, there is a free flow of material from the United States to Canada, and it was necessary to prevent that freedom being used as an indirect method of exporting United States goods from that country contrary to their export control legislation.
Commodities fall within three broad classifications for export control purposes. The first list covers items under control for all destinations and includes all items on which it is necessary to restrict or deny movement to the United States to maintain adequate domestic supply within Canada. It will be appreciated that in the type of article affected, such as scrap materials, it could easily happen that this Canadian market could be denuded if export controls were not maintained against the United States as well as all other countries.
List No. 2 is a list of items under export control to destinations other than the United States, and comprises those items which may be in short supply, and also a large number of strategic materials. Commodities within this group may move freely between Canada and the United States, but they cannot be exported without licence to other destinations from either country. An illustration of this

might be raw cotton, which moves from the United States to Canada without restriction, but which the United States and Canada have under export control to other destinations.
The third list is a list of countries exports to which require permits, or to which there is a general control of exports required. It is true that there is a very small list of items for export to these countries that is exempt. However, that list is quite small, and the items in it have no strategic significance whatever. This area control at present affects exports only, and does not affect imports.
The export powers under the existing act may be summarized under four headings. Those four headings are:
(a)	To establish a list of countries, exports to which shall be subject to licence.
(b)	To control exports of arms, munitions, war materials or supplies.
(c)	To control exports of commodities where this is necessary to ensure adequate supply and distribution within Canada, and
(d)	To control exports where this is necessary to implement inter-governmental arrangements or commitments.
So much for the exports part of the existing legislation.
Then, as to imports: When the act was passed initially in 1947, there were one hundred items under import control. These had been reduced to the point where at the end of 1950 no items were left under import control. Since the first of the year it has been necessary again to bring some items under import control. These are basic steel products on which control was imposed in order to direct the flow of imported steel into essential uses in compliance with the minister's orders issued under the Essential Materials (Defence) Act.
The authority or powers under the existing act, as they affect imports, may be subdivided into two headings:
(a)	To regulate or control the import of commodities subject to allocation by intergovernmental arrangement, governmental controls in the country of origin or scarcity in the world markets, and
(b)	To control imports where the price of the commodity is supported within the Canadian, market, under existing legislation.
The purpose of the amendments in the bill before the house may be set out briefly under three subheadings. The first is to extend the life of the act for three years, until July 31, 1954. I may add that a provision in that respect in the bill as originally drafted and submitted to parliament made provision for extension for five years. In the other place 80709-99i

Secondly, the bill empowers the governor in council to establish a list of countries, imports from which may be controlled, in order to enable Canada to implement obligations which may be incurred through international action. Hon. members will recall how some months ago there was discussion of international action which would affect imports as well as exports. We had no authority under any existing legislation to implement such a policy, had we agreed to it or had there been any international action making it desirable or necessary.
Then the third authority set out in the bill is that for imposing import controls where the production, supply, distribution or use of the article is restricted or otherwise regulated under the authority of any act of parliament. As an illustration, if it becomes necessary to regulate or prohibit the manufacture or distribution of certain products, it will be apparent to hon. members that it would be desirable to be able to exercise a similar control over an import trade in the same products. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make some comments about this bill to amend the Export and Import Permits Act. Here we have another control measure which is being placed before us because of the situation in which we find ourselves. This measure is really ancillary to the broader measures which we have already had before us during this session. It represents a considerable extension of the measure which we have had on the statute books under the same name since 1947, in particular because this bill now asks for authority to control imports on a country basis as well as on a commodity basis. As I say, it is a bill involving a great extension and before I take my seat I propose to move an amendment that the bill be sent to a committee so that its effect may be studied. I

Export and Import Permits Act suggest that the extensions which are being made are of great importance. When the act was made law four years ago it was considered carefully by a committee.
One of the things to which I wish to draw particular attention is that this measure has been used-I think it is desirable that we should know whether it is proposed to be used again-for purposes of discrimination. Let me hasten to say that I do not use that word in any sinister sense at all. I merely mean that the control powers have been used, as I shall show in a minute, to enable controllers to determine that Manufacturer A is more worthy of getting import materials than Manufacturer B. That is one reason why I think it is desirable that this measure should go to a committee. Then that aspect of the matter can be considered.
In order to make clear what I mean by that I should like to read briefly from the proceedings of the banking and commerce committee of 1947 when this act was first considered. What I am proposing to show is what I indicated a moment ago, that the powers have been used for the purposes of discriminating and judging that this manufacturer is more worthy of getting material than that manufacturer. Lest I forget, let me say that the civil servants who came before that committee won the respect and admiration of us all. It was perfectly evident that they were trying to do their job in a faithful and efficient manner. I am not criticizing them; rather I am criticizing the whole conception that these powers are being put in the hands of people, I do not care how good they are.
During the course of the evidence given by Mr. Bull the question of bench vises came up. I quote from the evidence given by Mr. Bull, as reported on page 295 of the proceedings:
On this question of bench vises, applications have been turned down on bench vises fairly generally because the bench vise is an article of very simple manufacture.
Then later on:
There is a minimum amount of machining going into a bench vise so that the price, on export, is not a great deal more than the price of the raw steel going into it. These vises are going to Holland where we never sold bench vises in the past and it is very doubtful if we will ever sell them in the future. We have difficulty competing in an article of simple manufacture. We usually do much better in a complex piece, such as a generator or a motor.
That outlines briefly the situation I am drawing attention to. I asked a question regarding it and then later Mr. Mackenzie, the deputy minister, made a statement which covered the point in a rather comprehensive manner. I quote from page 296 as follows:

(Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood).]
of the general policy of those unfortunate people who have to administer export permits. Where we have a very small supply to meet a large demand we have to make some decision and some choice because everybody's demands cannot be met. One of the guiding principles is that token shipments should go to those markets where it appears that there will be some continuing value. Mr. Bull pointed out that In the case of these items which require a very small amount of manufacturing in Canada, and are only one degree removed from the raw material, it is highly improbable that under more normal conditions, if those ever come, that we will be able to compete with manufacturers much closer to the markets. -to try to direct what limited supply there was to the markets where we thought there was some advantage.
I bring that before the house to indicate how powers taken for the purpose of controlling quantities can easily be used-I am perfectly sure in good faith-for the purpose of discriminating between one person and another. I hope that we can pursue this matter further when we get into committee because it seems to me to be dangerous in the highest degree that anyone should be asked to undertake the responsibility of making such a decision. The parliamentary assistant pointed out to us this afternoon what was satisfactory to hear, that the items under control under the old act had sunk to a very small number. But with the situation that has recently developed and our need for defence preparations, the number of articles under control will rise and have risen very substantially.
We should remember that we may be stepping into legislation which may go on for years and years. I suppose the best hope we can have is that it will go on for years and years because the alternative probably is war. When we remember that, it seems to me that these things should be carefully considered. I say again that this is discrimination, whether it is beneficial discrimination or not. Apparently we are giving the power to government officials to determine as between one person and another. They will have to have wisdom which I suggest is beyond all human wisdom. In addition they will have to be absolutely detached and impartial.
I should like to say a word or two about the public aspect of this. Do not think I deceive myself into believing that there is as yet any real apprehension on the part of the public as to the wide powers which parliament has granted. However, we in the opposition have questioned these powers because we consider it to be our duty to do so. I consider it to be my duty to go on trying to make people realize just what is happening, because it makes a very great deal

of difference whether the public says to itself, "These arbitrary powers are things we do not like; nevertheless the situation is such that we must give them. But we will watch exactly how they are exercised, and we will be on guard to try to diminish them as soon as the situation warrants." That is one thing, but that is not the situation we have in this country at the moment, as far as I can see. There is very little evidence 1 can detect outside this house, and not very much inside it, to suggest that anyone fears these powers. Therefore I am going to take a few moments of the time of the house to stress this point and put on record one or two quotations from people who have thought deeply about these matters, in the hope that they may come to the attention of members of the public, perhaps leaders of public opinion, who may be impelled to do something about it.
When I say that, I recognize that broad powers have to be given at the moment. Without them we cannot meet the issues we are facing now. What I am hoping is that they can be given in a considered way, so that people will recognize that it is a dangerous thing to do, and it is only done when you are in danger so great that you have to give up liberties-temporarily, we hope

which have cost much in the winning. For that reason I propose to quote a sentence or two from a man whose name is very well known and whose opinions are highly regarded. I refer to Walter Lippmann, and I am quoting from page 332 of his book "The Good Society". He is speaking about arbitrary powers, and we must remember that these powers are arbitrary. Although the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said the other day, and I am sure sincerely, that these great and arbitrary powers would be used with moderation, nevertheless we should remind ourselves that even in the hands of good men powers are sometimes used for purposes for which they were not intended. It was not the wicked Hitler who began the use of arbitrary power in governing by decree in Germany; it was the good Briining who began it. He was driven into it not because he wanted to but because he felt the circumstances warranted it, so it was he who really destroyed the German constitution, though he was a good and well-meaning man. Now I quote briefly from Lippmann:
The idea of arbitrary power exercised at the wilful discretion of any man is alien to the very conception of a civilized society. It is the legalism of the barbarian, and the instinctive political1 philosophy of all who have not been disciplined to, or are in reaction against, the usages of civilization. For every man, until he has been taught differently, is predisposed to believe that what he wills should have the force of law.

The struggle to subdue this primitive disposition is the age-old struggle against the barbarian.
I quote this passage from Lippmann, as I said, because of my feeling that it is our duty to try to make the people understand what is going on, so they will realize that the powers being given are far-reaching and could easily be very dangerous and harmful. I wish now to quote briefly from "The New Despotism" by Lord Hewart. At page 150 he quotes from a speech by the Master of the Rolls, who said that-
-time was when the great danger against which the judicature had to guard was the encroachments of the crown. Happily there was no longer that danger; but there was another danger which was more real than that-namely, encroachment by the executive.
As 1 say, I am bringing this to the attention of the house in order to get it on the record and call it to the attention of the people who also, I hope, may be led to reflect on these matters. Now I want to read just one other short passage from Lord Hewart, where he speaks about the delegation of authority and the position of the official who is endowed with these powers and exercises them. He says:
More than that, it is his duty, as an official, to obey any instructions given him by his superiors, and, in the absence of special instructions, to further what he knows to be the policy of his department. His position makes it inevitable that he should be subject to political influences.
I do not think the writer means that the official himself will be directly subject to political influences. I think he means that you have this power in the hands of a minister; men being what they are, the minister is a politician, and in that way political influences are bound to come in.
As I pointed out in the case of a similar measure, if this power was being asked for a month, a year, or any short time, one would feel quite differently about it; but none of us believes that three years from now, when this measure comes up for renewal, there will not be the slightest chance of taking the legislation off the statute books, unless the situation has changed radically. Therefore I think it is proper and indeed inescapable that we should think about this in terms of something that may go on for many years, and which may become part of the whole fabric of special powers that we have constructed. When I imagine that going on for such a period of time it is almost impossible for me, at any rate, to believe that we will have a generation which even knows how to practise the arts of freedom, and I am speaking now about freedom in the realm of economic enterprise.

As I apprehend the practice, there is a well established custom that the minister of a department speaks on behalf of his department, and that there is a special reason for his giving certain explanations and undertakings related to the principle of joint cabinet responsibility. Without in any way questioning the capacity of any individual member to deal with any particular subject, I think a question is now raised that should be considered without our waiting any longer. So far as I am aware, this is only the second department in which the parliamentary assistant has dealt with legislation before the house, and, in the process of dealing with legislation before the house, has been called upon to give explanations and what would amount to undertakings that would, in the ordinary course of events, be regarded as binding the government as to its intention in relation to that legislation.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that there is a long established reason for ministers giving that explanation, which has no suggestion of a reflection on the capacity of any other individual member of the house, but it does relate to the fact that only ministers can speak for the government. In this particular instance we are dealing with very important legislation. It is apparent that the parliamentary assistant in this instance has taken pains to inform himself in regard to the details of the measure before the house, and he has obviously made an earnest effort to give the explanations which he thinks are appropriate.
I submit, however, that he is not in a position to bind the government as to its intentions; I submit also that the government would be free from any measure of responsibility in

It is not the first time the hon. member has suggested that things we were doing may be all right, but that we were doing them in the wrong way. That was one of the very frequent notes sounded when he first came to the house. Recently we have not heard it so frequently.
But perhaps we might not hear the kind of suggestion he made this evening if he read the form of the legislation in which he himself participated. It is not in force for this fiscal year, because the estimates for 1952 have not'been adopted yet. But the item in question is couched in the same language as was used the first time the appointment of parliamentary assistants was decided upon, and ratified by the house.
The vote in this year's estimates, proposed to the house is in the same language as has been voted for many years, reads as follows:
To provide hereby, notwithstanding anything contained in the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act or the provisions of the Senate and House of Commons Act respecting the independence of parliament, for the payment out of the consolidated revenue fund to each member of the House of Commons appointed by the governor in council to be a parliamentary assistant (which appointment shall not render such member ineligible or disqualify him as: a member of the House of Commons) to assist a minister of the crown in such manner and to such extent as the minister may determine and to represent his department in the House of Commons in the absence of the minister therefrom, a salary of four thousand dollars per annum and pro rata for any period less than a year.
In previous years this has been part of the statutory legislation of this country, and I suggest that it is apt to be part of the statutory legislation of this country for the fiscal year 1951-52. It provides that the parliamentary assistant is to assist the minister of the crown in such manner and to such extent as the minister may determine, and to represent his department in the House of Commons in the absence of the minister therefrom.
That seems to me to justify the minister in asking his parliamentary assistant to take over the duty of supplying the information that may be required in the discussion of a bill such as this. The fact that the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Defence Production is here, and gave the explanation on second reading of the bill, and the fact

"that he is answering questions with respect to the bill in committee stage, should be sufficient proof that his minister has indicated that that is the manner and the extent to which he wished to have his assistance, in this instance, in return for the stipend of $4,000 a year provided in this vote.
I was here during the whole time this discussion in committee has taken place, and it did not appear to me that there was any undertaking being requested. Of course the practice is to have motions submitted by one of the minister's colleagues; because when a minister proposes second reading of his bill, or proposes any forward movement of his bill, he proposes it in the form in which it is submitted; and if there is to be any amendment, then under our rules he is not competent to move it himself.
Until parliament revokes this practice of there being parliamentary assistants, I suggest that the manner in which they have dealt with the business of the departments to which they have been appointed has, so far, been very satisfactory; and that if and when any undertaking is required, such as for instance the undertaking that is given when supplementary estimates are voted, that is always given by the minister of the department concerned. If in the course of the discussion of any of the measures before the house an undertaking were required, the question of its being given could be properly referred, by the parliamentary assistant supplying the information, to his minister, for that undertaking. If it were given by the parliamentary assistant, and were not an undertaking the government was prepared to respect, I suggest the one who had given it would not long remain a parliamentary assistant.

The explanations given as to the effect of the legislation and as to how it may be employed, and as to what the intention of the government is in regard to it, and the necessity for it, all form part of the pattern of a very loose system of dealing in an emergency with matters of this kind in a manner that ordinarily would not be regarded as acceptable to members of the house.

The Prime Minister has referred to provision that is made for parliamentary assistants and he has stated that a parliamentary assistant may be named who, under the direction of the minister, will carry out certain duties on behalf of a department. He has pointed out also that in the provision for parliamentary assistants it is explained that the parliamentary assistant shall represent the department or may represent the department in the absence of the minister.
There is a difference between representing a department and making explanations which amount to expressions of the government's opinion as to how something shall be done, or what the extent and effect of legislation will be. I have raised this point but I do not intend to press it further at this time. I suggest that it would be well when we are dealing with emergency legislation to be careful that we do know that the government is bound by such explanations or undertakings as are given, and it was with that in mind that I raised the question tonight.
We have had other emergency legislation before the house already and we may have more before the session is concluded. I suggest, having regard to the reasons why ministers speak on behalf of the government, bound as they are by a special oath of office and by special traditional responsibilities, that where explanations are to be given which will have great effect upon the business of this country and upon the understanding of the legislation that is being passed in very loose form, but granting very wide powers,

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 80, to amend the Migratory Birds Convention Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the Migratory Birds Convention Act, which was originally enacted in 1917, implements the migratory birds treaty between Canada and the United States. The treaty is similarly implemented in the United States by act of congress.


The treaty and the implementing acts were intended to preserve the various migratory birds which cross the international boundary each year; and as is well known to hon. members the treaty and its implementing acts have served their basic purpose.
It is not proposed at this time to make any substantive changes in the act. There are, however, a few minor matters which require amendment in order that the act and the machinery established for its administration may continue to perform in the best possible way the functions for which they are intended.
Subsection 2 of section 5 presently provides that persons who are appointed game officers by the minister responsible for the act or who are, as in the case of members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, game officers ex officio, hold office during pleasure and have the powers and duties defined by the act and regulations. Legal opinion is that this subsection is unnecessary, and it is therefore proposed to repeal it.
It is also proposed to repeal subsections 5 and 6 of section 5 and to replace both subsections by a subsection to be numbered 4. The purpose of this consolidation is to make it clear that all the provinces of Canada are on the same footing with respect to the appointment of game officers. Subsection 5 in its present form was placed in the act because the province of Ontario was the first province to indicate its desire that its game officers appointed under the Ontario Game Act should also act as game officers under this act. Subsection 6 was later added when other provinces made similar requests. The present proposed consolidation does not alter the scope or effect of these subsections but does provide for uniformity of treatment of all provinces in respect of the appointment of provincial game officers as game officers under this act.
The principal amendment embodied in the present bill is the amendment proposed to section 7 of the act. In recent years it has become clear that, with the increased use of motor vehicles and aircraft in hunting migratory birds, these means of transportation should be specifically included among the articles which, if used in committing violations of the act, can be seized by game officers. I may say that most of the provinces have already amended their provincial game acts to accomplish this purpose; and the amendment now proposed to the Migratory Birds Convention Act was requested by the 1950 conference of federal and provincial wildlife officers, in which the principal game administrators of the provinces took part.

I understand that the successful administration of this legislation depends upon the co-operation between the provincial and federal governments. So far as British Columbia is concerned, I understand that that co-operation has been extended and has been very successful.
I should like to say that the game commission of British Columbia, which has done excellent work throughout the years in connection with this act and other acts regulating the conservation of game, has been assisted to a great extent by the rod and gun clubs of British Columbia, which are very well organized now, and which throughout the years have done a great deal to develop public opinion in support of game conservation and the conservation of our natural resources.
Without a doubt, Mr. Speaker, my experience has been-and I have had some considerable experience with rod and gun clubs and fishing and hunting, and things of that sort, living in the country in which I do- that this type of legislation cannot be successfully administered by even the federal or the provincial authorities unless it has the support of, shall I say, a good percentage of people interested in these problems; and that is exactly what has happened in British Columbia. In British Columbia great credit is due to the rod and gun clubs of the province for their co-operation with the authorities and with the game commission, and for their advice and their assistance throughout the years. In fact in British Columbia the game commission depends to a great extent upon the recommendations forwarded to it by rod and gun clubs of that province.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, that the constituency I have the honour to represent has one of the most active organizations of that type in the province of British Columbia. For years these people have worked to build a public opinion in- support of the conservation of our wildlife and of our natural resources. That was not so in the early days. In the early days game was very plentiful; fish was very plentiful; wildlife in general was plentiful. As a result of overshooting

and overfishing there came a period when the stocks of game, of fish and of wildlife were sadly depleted. Then a small number of people began to take an interest and these organizations were formed. The result today is a very satisfactory administration of our game laws in British Columbia in co-operation with large numbers of people organized, as I said before, in the rod and gun clubs of that province.
Another interesting feature of the development in my province is the interest that has been stimulated among younger people, junior members of the rod and gun clubs. These young people enter fishing competitions, and join- in the activities to a great extent of the adult clubs in fishing and hunting under supervision, and are inculcated with the idea of the value of -our game and natural resources. It is a wonderful training ground for sportsmanship, and sportsmanship is a basic requirement of a sound and functioning democracy.
I am very glad to see the amendments mentioned in this bill, particularly the one with respect to extending the powers of the game officer to seize motor vehicles or aircraft which had been or are being used in violation of the act or any regulation under the act. I am particularly pleased to say that because personally even in recent years I have seen some rather ghastly things happen so far as game is concerned because we had not a section like this in this -act or in similar acts. I have seen American sportsmen come from the eastern United States to our district. They come in a car, or one of those vans, filled with dogs. I have seen them spend days driving through the mountain valleys, with their dogs trained to drive the grouse toward the road. They will go down the centre of the road for about thirty miles or so, and the dogs are trained to drive the birds toward the highway. Those men can sit in their motor vehicle or, if the occasion requires, get out of it quickly, and shoot grouse in wholesale quantities.
The amendment will prevent this sort of thing, so far as the migratory birds are concerned. I have seen power boats used in the shooting of geese and ducks in large numbers. This amendment will remedy that situation.
Only three years ago I saw a light aircraft used to fly around the peaks of some of our mountains, for the purpose of spotting herds of mountain goat which were sheltered on ledges facing the sun, as they usually do in the afternoon. Those aircraft would spot the herds of goat, and then land on a nearby lake. Following that the sportsmen could

go directly up to where the goats were, and shoot them in great numbers.
That is not sportsmanship. This measure would not apply in that case, but I mention it only to indicate the problem we have to face in connection with the conservation of game. In conclusion may I say that this group welcomes these amendments, and we trust the minister and his officials will have every co-operation, as in the past, in giving effect to these improvements in the act.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think anyone could complain about the suggested amendments, so long as they will help in the preservation of game. I do not believe the minister intended that this bill should become the occasion for a full-scale debate on the Migratory Birds Convention Act. At the same time we are well aware of the fact that when the estimates are before the committee, and the expenditure in connection with this act is called, it is met by hurried cries of "carried, carried, carried," from the government side, and from all who are anxious to finish the work.
However, I intend to have more to say about the matter at that time. In view of the fact that it may be some time before the estimates are called, I would put this to the minister: I have become aware-and I believe I am not far off the mark-that the migratory birds convention is not being observed by all who are signatories to it. I refer particularly to Mexico, and to some other countries in the south where commercial shooting is carried on. I suggest to the minister that, in view of the fact that there may be discussion later, in which certainly I intend to participate, he should obtain information regarding those countries.
I have been a duck shooter for years. However, last year I called the minister's attention to the fact that the season was altogether too late in our section of the country. Local ducks had gone, with the result that when the season was called we had no shooting of northern ducks. I would agree readily to a closed season if it would do any good, but as I see it-and I have made this statement in the house before-while the provinces are doing a good job of conservation, and doing everything they can to preserve game, all that work is being done at a loss if we preserve the birds in this country only to have them shot farther south.
Anyone who is familiar with duck shooting knows it is much easier to do the shooting in the United States because they know the time, almost to the hour, when the northern ducks will fly into their locality, at which time they will be waiting in the marshes to shoot them.

I still believe however that the department in the United States is trying to do a good job. They have made limitations as to the number of ducks to be taken, and their game wardens have acted efficiently. The trouble begins farther south, however. Before we have any further debate on the Migratory Birds Convention Act, as it may develop when the estimates are before the committee, I would suggest that the minister would do well to make some inquiries-I am sure he has the means at hand to do so-as to whether we are accomplishing all we might accomplish in North America and in the Caribbean countries to preserve game. I am wondering if some attempt could be made to bring those countries within the provisions of the migratory birds convention.
If commercial shooting exists in the West Indies and in Mexico, then let us have that fact out in the open and do something about it. We are not responsible for the administration of law in those countries; but as matters now stand there can be no doubt that they do have commercial shooting, and that we are protecting ducks that we ourselves are not getting a chance to shoot.
I have said I would agree to a closed season, if it would help. I do not think the fault is with the United States, but I do believe we should do something to get the countries I have mentioned under the provisions of the migratory birds convention. In this way we would be doing something to preserve game. However, so long as we protect ducks in our northern areas, while commercial shooting exists in other areas, we will have difficulties.
The ducks from our northern areas fly over here, and a certain amount of shooting is done. I have never found our sportsmen unreasonable; they have never gone in for wholesale slaughter. I believe a good job is being done in the United States, but I still feel that the convention cannot work effectively so long as commercial shooting exists in those other countries. In those southern areas there is a large influx of people during the winter months. They are not opposed to eating canvas backs or black ducks, if they can be obtained or bought-and I believe that is going on. I do not think we will ever accomplish anything until that practice is stopped.
I make the suggestion that, in preparing his estimates, the minister make further inquiries along these lines. We have done and are doing in Canada what we can to clear up this affair; and I believe the United

Migratory Birds Convention Act States are doing something-although large numbers of ducks perish each year from oil slicks on the eastern coast.
The whole situation is changing rapidly, and I do not find myself as optimistic as the hon. member who spoke a moment ago. The duck population is going down. However, I said at the outset I would not speak at length. My suggestion is that the minister get further information as to what can be done with respect to those Caribbean countries in which commercial shooting is permitted. In this way we would be getting down to the root of the matter.
I approve of everything in Bill No. 80. Any means we can take to stop unsportsmanlike practices in dealing with wild or migratory birds is a step in the right direction. I believe the provinces are doing a good job. While I give the bill my wholehearted support and approval, I would leave the suggestion I have made with the minister.

However, when the Auditor General of Canada deals with the public accounts he goes a bit further and deals with matters that, shall I say, at least border on questions of policy. The Auditor General not only gives us a statement as to the fact that he has seen all the vouchers he wanted to see, but he gives us that interesting report that is furnished each year at the end of the big book known as the public accounts, in which he points out any seeming irregularities which he feels should be drawn to the attention of parliament, whose servant the Auditor General is.
I feel that we should have that kind of auditing job done with respect to the work of the Canadian National Railways, and it is for that reason it does seem to me that, instead of hiring a private firm, we should arrange for the auditing of the accounts of the Canadian National Railways, and its various subsidiary bodies, to be done by the Auditor General of Canada. I would be glad to hear from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), either at this stage of the debate or when we get into committee, as to whether any further consideration has been given to this matter, and if so what is the result of that consideration.

Addressing myself to the suggestion made by the member for Winnipeg North Centre, I should say that parliament has provided for the method in which the audit shall take place. The provision is set out in section 13 of the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act, 1933, as amended by the act of 1936. In effect it states that a continuous audit of the accounts of national railways shall be made by independent auditors appointed annually by a resolution of parliament and annually reporting to parliament in respect of their audit. What the meaning of that is, I believe, is as clear to the hon. member as it is to me. I think an independent group of auditors-

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF GEORGE A. TOUCHE AND COMPANY AS AUDITORS
speechtext: Surely the Auditor General is independent.

speechtext:
I think an independent
group of auditors means exactly what it says. While it may be true that it does not exclude the Auditor General, there are reasons other than those contained in section 13, why the government has seen fit to continue to submit to parliament an independent firm of auditors, such as the one recommended in this bill. I do not want to repeat what I have said on earlier occasions, because this is not the first time that the suggestion has been made. It has been made on more than one occasion, and there are compelling reasons against it. For instance, the Auditor General would have to set up quite a financial staff of men to do the work which is being done by this firm of auditors, or which could be done by some other firm. Certainly it could not be said that there would be any curtailment of expenditure by the appointment of the Auditor General. In fact, the studies that we have made in our department lead us to believe that the cost would be greater by the appointment of the Auditor General than by the appointment of an independent firm such as is mentioned in the bill.
Another thing that has to be kept in mind is that this is a continuous audit. Whether or not it is done by the Auditor General, it would take him some time to familiarize himself with the various units and establishments of the Canadian National Railways; that is not done overnight. These people have been at it for years. Then again, the Canadian National Railways operates various units outside of Canada in Duluth, St. Albans, Chicago, and other points in the United States which do not come to my mind at the


moment. The firm that is mentioned in this bill have offices in these United States cities. The Auditor General would have to establish some such staff in those cities in order to audit adequately the accounts of the railway. Those are the main reasons that come to my mind at the moment and which I think militate against the appointment of the Auditor General. For that reason I must tell the committee that I would have to oppose the suggestion.

I was interested in what the hon. member for Greenwood had to say just now as to the desirability of having in that independent report, whoever makes it, a more comprehensive kind of thing than we now get, something more like that which we get from the Auditor General when he audits the public accounts. That is a suggestion made, as I say, by the hon. member whom I am quoting. My point is that I think we could get a more independent audit by the Auditor General who is the servant of this parliament and who is used to making the kind of report he is making, than we get from a private firm of auditors whose main interest, after all, is in bookkeeping accuracy and that sort of thing.
The Minister of Transport says that we might not save any money by having the audit done by the Auditor General, because he would have to take on additional staff to do the job now being done by George A. Certainly the Auditor General would have to expand his staff to do this job; and I grant what the Minister of Transport says, namely, that it might cost us just as much to do it that way as to do it the other way; it might even cost more. But surely what we must look at is not just the actual cost of the audit but the results we would get from that audit. It might be worth more to have the kind of audit of the accounts of the Canadian National Railways that we get from the Auditor General with respect to the public accounts.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is anything very contentious in the bill but the minister might explain it.

maintopic: RADIO ACT, 1938 VARIOUS AMENDMENTS  DEFINITION OF TELECOMMUNICATION    ACCESSION TO INTERNATIONAL CONVENTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes; I was going to do that. The purpose of this bill is to carry out and implement the terms of an agreement, in fact it is a treaty, made between Canada and the United States covering several matters in connection with radio. That is, the agreement made between the two countries was made in order to permit, first, pilots who are qualified radio operators to operate radio transmitters installed in civilian airplanes of the other country's registry; second, operators of mobile radio transmitters installed in vehicles used in public service or for commercial purposes in border areas and private persons with radio telephony installed in their cars while in the territory of the other country; and third, amateur wireless operators to use their sets while visiting the other country.
Section 5 of the act of 1938, which provides for the licensing of stations, is repealed by this amendment, and the new section provides for the necessity of a licence in the case of the operation of a private receiving station or a radio station by the making of regulations by the governor in council so that (a) radio receiving sets installed in an automobile or other vehicles and (b) a radio station temporarily in Canada may by these regulations be exempted from the operation of section 5 of the act.
Section 7 of the act of 1938 provides that no one shall be employed as a radio operator on any coast, land or mobile station unless he is a British subject, and also makes provision for the taking of an oath of secrecy. The amendment to that section permits the exemption by regulation of the classes mentioned in the treaty which are (a) radio operators employed on any radio station in Canada or (b) any person who holds a valid Canadian certificate of proficiency or an equivalent certificate issued by the country of which he is a citizen, and (c) is a citizen and resident of a country that grants a reciprocal permission to Canadian citizens.
In other words, the matters I have referred to so far are to implement the treaty entered into between Canada and the United States. There are two other small amendments, one of which is a new one and gives a new definition of telecommunication, and the other amends section 3 (1) (c) of the act by substituting "telecommunication" for the word "radio" which is there now. It is simply to clarify the act and to permit of approval under international agreements of telecommunication regulations, telegraph regulations

and the like. I do not think there is anything contentious in the bill. I think it is all to the good. It was given careful consideration by the two countries and I hope it will commend itself to the house.
